title: Hierarchical budget ledger
description: Objective: implement immutable hierarchical account allocation and return over the contract from task-7dc2e4870d7d4096a1be7b5991e50e94. Deliverable: packages/scheduler/src/budget/budget-account.ts, its one-line .js bridge, and focused tests for root snapshots, parent-to-child allocation, child-to-current-parent return, balanced ledger entries, optimistic version fencing, derived subtree roll-up, replay, and legal closure. NOT in scope: work reservations, admission policy, usage measurements, settlement/quarantine, persistence, root authorization issuance, or package-root export. Hard dependency: task-7dc2e4870d7d4096a1be7b5991e50e94 must be DONE and its tests remain unchanged. Owned paths: budget-account.ts, budget-account.js, budget-account.test.ts. Verification: pnpm --filter @moe/scheduler typecheck && pnpm --filter @moe/scheduler exec vitest run --root ../.. packages/scheduler/src/budget/budget-account.test.ts.
definitionOfDone: Every accepted child allocation moves exactly the same integer units from parent AVAILABLE to child AVAILABLE, and every legal return performs the inverse without copying or sibling borrowing.

After each transition and replay, the derived root-plus-descendants AVAILABLE+RESERVED+QUARANTINED+COMMITTED total equals the authorized root amount plus explicit recorded overrun, with all direct buckets nonnegative safe integers.

Stale expected versions, missing/current-parent mismatches, insufficient AVAILABLE, duplicate identities, and illegal close states return deterministic frozen local issues with zero state or ledger-entry change.
A child closes only after returning direct AVAILABLE and proving direct RESERVED and QUARANTINED are zero; replay of canonical entries reconstructs the same deeply frozen state.
Both TypeScript files are <=250 physical lines, the bridge is one exact re-export line, and the focused verification command exits 0.

implementationPlan.description: Implement allocate, return and close in budget-account.ts. Validate every precondition BEFORE constructing any successor: resolve parent and child, fence expectedParentVersion and expectedChildVersion, confirm the child's stored parentRef equals the named parent, confirm the meter exists on both sides, confirm the amount is a positive safe integer within the parent's direct AVAILABLE, and confirm identities are not duplicated. Check in one published fixed order and let the FIRST failing check decide the single reported code, per lease-fencing.ts:87-95, so a rejection is deterministic. On any rejection return the prior state object itself — the same reference, with no entry appended — so no partial mutation is observable. On success build both successor records with their versions bumped, append exactly one balanced entry (ALLOCATED from parent to child, RETURNED from child to parent), and deep-freeze the new state before returning it; never mutate an existing record in place. closeBudgetAccount permits closure only when direct AVAILABLE, RESERVED and QUARANTINED are all zero and every child is already CLOSED; COMMITTED may be nonzero and the account is retained in state with state CLOSED so its committed units keep counting toward the derived total. Keep the child's meter list within MAX_BUDGET_METERS. Then add replayBudgetLedger(authorization, entries), which folds the canonical entries through the same transition core so replay cannot drift from live application, and create budget-account.js containing exactly the single line `export * from "./budget-account.ts";`.

GREEN. budget-account.ts at 250 physical lines, budget-account.test.ts at 250, budget-account.js at 1 (`export * from "./budget-account.ts";`). Typecheck exit 0; focused suite "Test Files 1 passed (1) / Tests 32 passed (32)", exit 0.

SHARED MOVEMENT CORE: allocateToChild and returnToParent are one-line wrappers over applyMovement(state, command, kind), so allocation and return cannot drift apart — they are literally the same code with source and sink swapped. ALLOCATED has source=parent/sink=child; RETURNED is the mirror. That is what makes "return is the exact inverse" structural rather than a coincidence of two hand-written functions.

PUBLISHED CHECK ORDER, first failure decides the single code, per lease-fencing.ts:87-95: malformed, duplicate identity, unknown account, exhausted counter, stale version, parent mismatch, unknown meter, insufficient available. All 22 rejection cases assert exactly one code, and one case deliberately trips several checks at once to prove the order is respected rather than accidental.

NOTHING IS CONSTRUCTED UNTIL EVERY CHECK PASSES, and every rejection returns `fail(state, ...)` carrying the SAME state reference with no entry appended. Successors are built with spreads over fresh bucket copies (`shift` maps to new objects and never mutates in place), then the whole state is deep-frozen. The suite proves this with reference identity (toBe) on all 22 cases, not deep equality.

SIBLING BORROWING IS STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE, on two independent grounds: the parent-mismatch check requires child.parentRef === the named parent, and there is no entry shape that credits without debiting the same amount from exactly one named account.

METER RULES: the source must always carry the meter; the sink must also carry it when returning, because a parent's meter set is authorized and must not autovivify. A child being funded MAY gain a meter — that is how a child acquires meters at all — and the resulting list is checked against MAX_BUDGET_METERS before acceptance.

VERSIONS: a movement bumps BOTH sides, except that a newly created child is born at version 0 rather than 1, since there is no prior version to advance. The counter-exhaustion guard refuses a mutation when either side is at MAX_BUDGET_VERSION, for the lease-fencing reason — a successor above the ceiling would produce a record that never parses again.

CLOSURE requires direct AVAILABLE, RESERVED and QUARANTINED all zero AND every child already CLOSED; COMMITTED may be nonzero. The account is RETAINED with state CLOSED, never removed, so its committed units keep counting in the derived total.

REPLAY folds canonical entries through applyMovement and closeBudgetAccount — the same core as live application — so it cannot drift. Versions are read from the state being rebuilt rather than from entries, because a version is a consequence of the fold.

ONE SEAM CHANGE I HAD TO MAKE, and it is the most important thing in this note. BudgetLedgerEntry needed a nullable `ownerRef` field beyond the plan's six. The plan fixed the entry shape as {sequence, kind, meter, amount, fromRef, toRef}, but I folded child creation into allocation in step 2, which makes the child's ownerRef a canonical fact of the creating movement that cannot be re-derived from any other field. Without it, replay reconstructs a child with the wrong ownerRef and the replay-equals-live test fails — I hit exactly that. `ownerRef` is populated only on the ALLOCATED entry that creates an account and is null elsewhere; the field carries a comment saying why. The alternative was a separate account-creation function and entry kind, which costs more lines and more surface for no benefit.

THREE TEST DEFECTS FIXED, two of which I predicted in step 4 by walking my check order against the table rather than waiting for red: "returning a meter the parent does not carry" passed expectedParentVersion 1 against a hand-built root at version 0, so it would have reported STALE_VERSION and silently proved nothing about meters; "closing a parent whose child is still open" ran against a root that still held AVAILABLE, so it reported ILLEGAL_CLOSE for the wrong reason and did not isolate the open-child rule — it now uses a drained root so the open child is the ONLY violation; and the two entry assertions gained the ownerRef field. All three are cases that would have passed while testing the wrong thing, which is precisely the defect class the new epic rail warns about.

implementationPlan.note:
Adversarial self-review and commit `406eb95` (3 files, 501 insertions, exactly the owned paths).

INCIDENT I CAUSED AND FIXED, reported first because it is the most important thing here. My first mutation harness restored the file with a naive `String.replace` whose needle was the bare token `false`. String.replace hits only the FIRST occurrence, and `false` appears earlier in the file, so the "restore" corrupted two places instead of reverting one: the result union's `readonly ok: false` was overwritten with the parent-mismatch expression, and the real parent-mismatch guard was left as `if (false)`. Because budget-account.ts was untracked at that moment there was no `git checkout` to fall back on. I found it by grepping for the mutation artefacts rather than assuming the restore worked, repaired both sites by hand, and re-verified: 250 lines, typecheck 0, 32/32 green. I then rebuilt the harness properly — a backup copied outside the repo, `split().join()` for whole-file replacement, and a `git hash-object` equality check after every restore. All three subsequent restores were byte-identical to baseline cef76cdc, and the backup was deleted. Lesson recorded for the handoff: never mutate a file with a common-token needle, and never mutate an UNTRACKED file without an out-of-tree backup.

MUTATION TESTING, which the new epic rail requires rather than merely suggests — a green suite proves nothing until you show it can go red. Three production mutations, each restored byte-identically:
- Parent-mismatch guard neutered -> 8 tests red. Note the honest detail: it reddened the happy paths rather than the sibling case, because my replacement expression also fires during legitimate child creation. It proves the guard is load-bearing, just by a different route than I predicted.
- Rejection returns a rebuilt `{...state}` instead of the same reference -> 8+ rejection tests red. This is the one I most wanted to prove, because deep equality would have passed and the whole "no partial mutation is observable" claim rests on it.
- Movement credits without debiting (`sign` dropped) -> 8 tests red including conservation, replay and the insufficient-available case.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
LEDGER MODEL — chosen: strict double-entry. Every BudgetLedgerEntry carries {sequence, kind, meter, amount, fromRef, toRef}. ALLOCATED is from=parent,to=child; RETURNED is from=child,to=parent; ROOT_OPENED is from=null,to=root (the external authorization named in task rail 2). "Balanced" then means literally: every entry debits exactly one account and credits exactly one account for the same integer amount, so per-meter conservation is a theorem of the entry shape rather than a check bolted on afterwards, and "no copying or sibling borrowing" is structurally impossible — there is no entry shape that credits without debiting.
Rejected — entries holding a post-state snapshot per account: replay becomes trivial but the entries stop being canonical movement facts, and conservation degrades to an assertion over snapshots.
Rejected — a scalar (non-per-meter) ledger: contradicts BudgetMeterBuckets, which is per-meter.

ISSUE REPORTING — mirror lease-fencing.ts:87-95: check in a published fixed order and let the FIRST failing check decide the code, so one rejected command never reports two causes and the outcome is deterministic. Reuse the contract's BudgetIssue {code, message} *shape* with a locally-declared code union.

CLOSURE — close requires direct available === 0, reserved === 0, quarantined === 0. COMMITTED may be nonzero: spent units are a real recorded fact and must keep counting toward the subtree total, so **closed accounts are never removed from state**. Also treat closing an account that still has non-CLOSED children as illegal; DoD says "illegal close states" without enumerating, and permitting it would strand a funded subtree. Flagged here so the approver can strike it if they consider it scope creep.

OVERRUN — settlement is explicitly out of scope, so no transition in this kernel can create overrun. Model it as an explicit per-meter `overrun` field initialised to 0 at root open and never raised here, and carry it as a term in the conservation equation (total === authorized + overrun). DoD item 2 names it, so it is in scope; keeping it explicit-but-inert is what lets the later settlement child raise it without reopening this file.

planningNotes.risks:
1. LINE BUDGET IS THE REAL RISK. 250 lines must hold types, cloned helpers, openRoot, allocate, return, close, derived roll-up and replay. My estimate is ~230-255, i.e. it can genuinely overflow. Compress the way budget-contract.ts already does — several declarations per physical line, one-line interface members — and lean on validateBudgetAccount() instead of re-validating fields. If it still will not fit WITHOUT dropping a DoD item, call moe.report_blocked and ask for a split. Do NOT silently drop a validation, a transition, or a test case to make the number.
2. Version fencing must bump BOTH sides. An allocation mutates parent and child, so the command carries expectedParentVersion AND expectedChildVersion and both must match before anything moves. Fencing only the parent is the obvious bug here.
3. Counter exhaustion: apply the lease-fencing.ts:111-118 idiom — refuse a mutation when a version is at the ceiling, because emitting a successor above it produces a record that never parses again. Define a local MAX ceiling; do not assume version can grow forever.
4. "Zero state or ledger-entry change" on rejection means validate EVERYTHING before mutating anything. Build the successor records first, and only then swap them into the new state — never mutate the parent and then discover the child is stale. The test must assert the rejected state is reference-identical (toBe) to the prior state, not merely deep-equal; deep equality would pass even if a fresh identical object had been rebuilt, and it would not catch a mutated-then-restored state.
5. -0 and unsafe integers: the contract's isCount deliberately rejects -0, NaN, Infinity and fractions. An allocation of 0 units is a legal no-op amount by isCount but is almost certainly not intended as a ledger entry — decide explicitly and freeze the decision in a test. Recommend rejecting a zero-amount allocation as a malformed command so the ledger never carries inert entries.
6. Per-meter, not scalar. A meter present on the child but absent on the parent, and a meter absent on both, are distinct cases and both must fail closed rather than autovivify a bucket. Allocating an unknown meter must not silently create it on the parent.
7. Replay must produce a DEEPLY frozen state and must equal the incrementally built state. Test it by constructing via transitions, capturing the entries, replaying them into a fresh state and asserting deep equality plus Object.isFrozen at more than the top level — a shallow freeze passes a lazy check and still lets a caller mutate a meter bucket.
8. MAX_BUDGET_METERS is 64 and the contract enforces it on parse. Do not let allocation grow a child's meter list past it.
9. Shared working directory: stage only the three owned paths. Do not touch budget-contract.* (task rail 1) and do not add anything to packages/scheduler/src/index.ts.

DoD 3 is proven at the strongest available level, worth naming because most suites settle for less: rejections assert `expect(result.state).toBe(prior)` — reference identity, not deep equality — plus unchanged entries length and a frozen issue. A kernel that mutated then rebuilt an identical object fails that.

DoD 4: replay deep-equals the incrementally built state, and freezing is checked at five levels (state, accounts, record, meters array, bucket), so a shallow freeze cannot pass.
